final_writeup:
Let K_p=complement(H_p) and n=(p−1)/2. I do not prove the requested limit. I obtain the exact Cayley/Fourier linear program, identify all of its Fourier data as real parts of Jacobi sums, and prove

((√p−1)(√p+3))/(2(√p+1)) ≤ θ(K_p) ≤ √p−1.

Consequently

1/√2 ≤ liminf θ(K_p)/√(p/2) ≤ limsup θ(K_p)/√(p/2) ≤ √2.

Moreover θ(H_p)θ(K_p)=n, so the target is exactly the assertion that these two complementary theta numbers become asymptotically balanced. In the projection formulation below, it is equivalent to proving that the largest possible trivial-coordinate mass of a nonnegative vector in an explicit half-dimensional cyclotomic Fourier subspace is asymptotic to n^(−1/2). Exact small cases are θ(K_5)=1, θ(K_13)=2, and θ(K_17)=8−4√2.

results.claim: Writing Q for the nonzero squares and K_p=complement(H_p), both H_p and K_p are Cayley graphs on the multiplicative group Q. Their connection sets S and T have sizes (p−5)/4 and (p−1)/4, respectively.
results.proof_sketch: For x,y∈Q, χ(x−y)=χ(y)χ(x/y−1)=χ(x/y−1). Thus S={q∈Q\{1}:χ(q−1)=1} and T={q∈Q:χ(q−1)=−1}. Both are inverse-closed because χ(q⁻¹−1)=χ(1−q)=χ(q−1), using χ(q)=χ(−1)=1. Also Σ_{q∈Q}χ(q−1)=−1: insert 1_Q(x)=(1+χ(x))/2 on F_p^*, and use Σ_{x≠0}χ(x−1)=−1 and Σ_xχ(x(x−1))=−1. Hence |S|−|T|=−1, while |S|+|T|=|Q|−1=(p−3)/2, giving the asserted sizes.

results.claim: The localized Paley sign matrix B has operator norm at most √p, by an exact conference-matrix identity.
results.proof_sketch: Let C_{xy}=χ(x−y) on F_p. The elementary quadratic-character correlation gives C²=pI−J. Choose a nonsquare ν and label the nonsquares by ν/q, q∈Q. In the ordering {0},Q,{ν/q:q∈Q}, C has blocks [[0,1ᵀ,−1ᵀ],[1,B,D],[−1,D,−B]], where B_{qr}=χ(q−r) and D_{qr}=χ(qr−ν) is symmetric. The Q,Q block of C²=pI−J yields B²+D²=pI−2J. Therefore, for every real v, ||Bv||²=p||v||²−2(1ᵀv)²−||Dv||²≤p||v||².

results.claim: θ(K_p) is exactly an explicit finite Fourier linear program, or equivalently a nonnegative-vector problem for a half-dimensional Fourier projection.
results.proof_sketch: Average any feasible theta matrix over multiplication by Q. It becomes X_{xy}=f(x⁻¹y)/n, where f(1)=1, f|_T=0, f(q)=f(q⁻¹), and all Fourier coefficients f̂(ψ) are nonnegative. Conversely these conditions make X feasible. Hence θ(K_p)=max Σ_qf(q). Put y_ψ=f̂(ψ)/n. Then y≥0, Σ_ψy_ψ=1, and θ(K_p)=n y_triv. If D={1}∪S, then |D|=n/2 and f|_{Q\D}=0 is equivalent to P_Dy=y, where P_D is the orthogonal Fourier projection onto functions supported on D. Thus θ(K_p)/n=max{y_triv:y≥0, Σy=1, P_Dy=y}, with conjugate coordinates identified.

results.claim: Every nontrivial Fourier eigenvalue of B is the real part of a Jacobi sum of modulus √p.
results.proof_sketch: For a nontrivial character ψ of Q, extend it to a character A of F_p^*. Its B-eigenvalue, up to replacing ψ by its conjugate, is R_ψ=Σ_{q∈Q}ψ(q)χ(q−1). Inserting the square indicator gives R_ψ=(J(A,χ)+J(Aχ,χ))/2. Gauss-sum identities give J(A,χ)J(Aχ,χ)=G(χ)²=p, while both Jacobi sums have modulus √p. They are therefore conjugates, so R_ψ=Re J(A,χ) and |R_ψ|≤√p. In particular, off the diagonal, (P_D)_{ψ,φ}=(1+R_{ψφ⁻¹})/(2n), while its diagonal is 1/2.

results.claim: For every vertex-transitive graph G on n vertices, θ(G)θ(complement(G))=n.
results.proof_sketch: The SDP dual is min t subject to tI+Z−J⪰0, with Z supported on edges. If M=tI+Z−J is dual feasible, then (M+J)/(nt) is primal feasible for the complement and has objective at least n/t; hence the product is at least n. Conversely, average an optimal primal X over a transitive automorphism group. Then diag(X)=1/n and X1=(θ(G)/n)1. The matrix (n²/θ(G))X−J is positive semidefinite and is a dual certificate for the complement with value n/θ(G). This proves the reverse inequality.

results.claim: Theta is monotone under taking induced subgraphs.
results.proof_sketch: A feasible matrix for an induced subgraph can be extended by zero rows and columns to the full graph, preserving positive semidefiniteness, trace, edge-zero constraints, and objective.

results.claim: Theta is additive on disjoint unions: θ(G⊔L)=θ(G)+θ(L).
results.proof_sketch: In Gram form, align the vector sums of optimal solutions for G and L and choose their scale factors proportional to the square roots of their theta values; this gives the lower bound. Conversely, for any feasible Gram family on the union, if its two block traces are a and b, the squared norms of the two block vector sums are at most aθ(G) and bθ(L). Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the total objective by (a+b)(θ(G)+θ(L))=θ(G)+θ(L).

results.claim: The full Paley graph P_p satisfies θ(P_p)=√p.
results.proof_sketch: Translations make P_p vertex-transitive. Multiplication by any nonsquare changes every square difference into a nonsquare difference, so P_p is isomorphic to its complement. The vertex-transitive product identity therefore gives θ(P_p)²=p.

Let N be the nonsquares. Multiplication by a nonsquare identifies K_p with the Paley subgraph P_p[N]. Vertex 0 has no Paley edges to N, so P_p[{0}∪N] is the disjoint union of one isolated vertex and K_p. Induced-subgraph monotonicity, additivity, and θ(P_p)=√p give 1+θ(K_p)≤√p.

H_p is d-regular with d=(p−5)/4. On 1⊥ its adjacency eigenvalues are (−1+R_ψ)/2, so its least eigenvalue τ is at least −(√p+1)/2. For a d-regular graph on n vertices, the dual matrix tI+cA−J gives θ≤−nτ/(d−τ): take c=n/(d−τ) and t=−nτ/(d−τ). Substitution of n=(p−1)/2, d=(p−5)/4, and −τ≤(√p+1)/2 gives the formula. For p=5, H_p is empty on two vertices and the same formula equals 2.

The upper bound was proved above. Since H_p is vertex-transitive and K_p is its complement, θ(H_p)θ(K_p)=n=(p−1)/2. Dividing n by the preceding upper bound for θ(H_p) gives θ(K_p)≥(√p−1)(√p+3)/(2(√p+1))=(√p+1)/2−2/(√p+1).

results.claim: The proven bounds imply 1/√2≤liminf θ(K_p)/√(p/2)≤limsup θ(K_p)/√(p/2)≤√2, and isolate the unresolved step as asymptotic balance of the complementary theta numbers.
results.proof_sketch: Divide the explicit bounds by √p/√2 and let p tend to infinity. Also θ(H_p)θ(K_p)=n and √n/√(p/2)→1. Thus the requested limit is equivalent to θ(K_p)/√n→1, to θ(H_p)/√n→1, or to θ(H_p)−θ(K_p)=o(√p). None of the proved estimates establishes this balance.

results.claim: The exact small-prime values are θ(K_5)=1, θ(K_13)=2, θ(K_17)=8−4√2; correspondingly θ(H_5)=2, θ(H_13)=3, and θ(H_17)=2+√2.
results.proof_sketch: For p=13, identify Q with Z/6Z; S={±1}. A Fourier-feasible function has values 1 at 0 and a at ±1. Its eigenvalues are 1+2a cos(πl/3); l=3 forces a≤1/2, and a=1/2 is feasible, giving 2. For p=17, Q≅Z/8Z and S={±1,4}. Write f(±1)=a and f(4)=b. The Fourier inequalities are 1+2a cos(πl/4)+b(−1)^l≥0. Taking a=2−√2 and b=3−2√2 is feasible and gives 8−4√2. Conversely, the nonnegative combination (4−2√2) times the l=3 inequality plus (3−2√2) times the l=4 inequality yields 2a+b≤7−4√2. Complementary values follow from the product identity.

results.claim: A tempting exact explanation—K_p being a relabelled copy of H_p with one perfect matching added—is already false for p=17.
results.proof_sketch: Here H_17=Cay(Z/8Z,{±1,4}) and K_17=Cay(Z/8Z,{±2,±3}). Since their degrees differ by one, such an extension would mean K_17−M≅H_17 for some perfect matching M. H_17 is triangle-free with four induced 4-cycles. Exact enumeration gives 14 perfect matchings of K_17: twelve deletions retain a triangle, while the two triangle-free deletions each have six induced 4-cycles. Hence none is isomorphic to H_17.
